items.title: Hinge damage suspected to be behind iPhone Duo screen cracks
items.content_html:
The cause behind a repeating pattern in the way a very small amount of iPhone Duo screen cracks may have been discovered, with a failing element of the hinge believed to be causing the most damage.

Since the launch of the iPhone Duo, there have been sightings of cracked screens within hours of its release. While infant device failures are to be expected for major product launches, there is an consistency in the way that the screen itself is cracking.

Observing videos such as the JerryRigEverything "test" and posts to Reddit show the screen cracks in a fairly typical manner when under stress. In quite a few instances, the fault develops at the crease line and spreads out horizontally to the edge.

The expectation is that it's the screen itself cracking during the bend, but there's also another component that may be the cause. If a video by YouTuber CuriousHagi is to be believed, it may be caused by a faulty hinge.

During his own testing, which involved a lot of dirt and stressing the screen by folding the hinge backwards, he tried to close the iPhone Duo, but it wouldn't shut. He then tried opening it back from its partially-closed state, only to hear a loud snap.

Like other instances, the screen shows a large white issue from the crease to one of the sides. However, the YouTuber went one stage further and took apart the damaged iPhone Duo to find out what caused it.

After ripping off the display, he closely inspected the hinge mechanism and discovered an element that had sheared at the same location as where the screen crack originated. It appears to be a hinge element that connects to an upper support plate.

It's pointed out that the hinge in question is a little thinner than the hinges above and below, making it more likely to break. Also, a further check on the hinge shows heavy crush marks on a nearby mechanism that may have played a part.

The underside of the display also has what appear to be an impact mark, probably caused by the broken hinge element making contact. The most logical result is that the hinge failed to mesh correctly, the section sheared, and then hit the display, cracking it.

While there are reports of screen failures, as well as a commonality indicating they're suffering from a specific issue, it is still a limited problem for Apple. There's no major online outcry as yet for screens breaking in a particular way.

That said, so far after launch, it's still a very small-scale issue.

A broken hinge element in the iPhone Duo - Image Credit: CuriousHagi/YouTube

On October 24, AppleInsider checked with sources we have worked with for over 15 years, inside Apple Genius bars at seven stores. Four of those stores are major flagships.

At that time, none of the stores we polled had seen any devices in for service or returned because of broken screens. A secondary check late on Sunday revealed there is only one instance across all of the stores.

The number will increase over time, but it's not yet clear if the per capita will. So far it's not as widespread of a problem as the sensationalist videos propose.

As a reminder, it's not advised to abuse the hinge of the iPhone Duo by bending it backwards, even in curiosity, unless you're prepared to pay for repairs.

And, if yours breaks, report it to Apple. They do not listen to Reddit, or social media.

items.title: Touch-friendly dynamic interface coming soon to macOS Golden Gate
items.content_html:
The touch-enabled MacBook Pro will bring with it some changes to macOS Golden Gate, with a dynamic interface that will be better for finger-based navigation.

It's safe to say that the macOS interface is generally geared towards the mouse and keyboard, with touch securely in third place. However, the inbound MacBook Pro update with a touchscreen is forcing Apple to adjust macOS.

According to Mark Gurman in Sunday's "Power On" newsletter for Bloomberg, macOS Golden Gate will be tweaked for finger-based usage. This includes the introduction of a dynamic interface.

Gurman describes this as a system that will take previous interactions into account, with controls presented based on whether the users has been touching the display or the trackpad. This probably means the UI will vary between a more touch-centric version or one better suited for a cursor.

Touching buttons will also bring up menus around a user's finger for quick selection. The Dock and Menu Bar will also be optimized for tounch input, too.

The ultimate aim is to allow users to switch between touch and trackpad inputs without needing to think about it too much.

This is not the first time we have heard about touch-based changes in macOS. References in a macOS 27.2 beta in early October discussed touch gestures and touch-based dragging, as well as a "touch sentinel recognizer."

At the time, while it could've been an indicator of a touch-enabled MacBook Pro being on the way, it may have also been an update to better suit Sidecar.

items.title: Ternus shuffles more Apple roles as long-time executives look to retire
items.content_html:
A new report says there are again multiple staffing changes in key roles at Apple as the company promotes from within to cover retiring executives.

This isn't another case of half a dozen people leaving Apple in the lurch, chiefly because it's actually a managed changeover ahead of people retiring.

According to Bloomberg, the main people concerned are Wei Chen and John Zhong, both of whom worked on Apple's display technology. Chen took over Touch ID back in 2023 when its previous head retired.

Now both Chen and Zhong are reportedly stepping back from their leadership roles and instead becoming advisors. It's intended to be a transition for them after more than thirty years working for Apple, and of course to pass on those decades of experience to others.

That handover is said to have already begun, though. The two have been mentoring Victor Yin to replace at least some of their roles for some years.

As well as turning to existing Apple employees to eventually replace these two executives when they retire, the company has also made separate promotions. Reportedly this is part of an annual Apple series of promotions, but the key ones this time are all people working in internet connectivity.

Rajesh Ambati, Louie Sanguinetti and Derek Shaeffer have now all been promoted to vice president status. Sanguinetti Is described as an Apple lifer who has worked in wireless hardware.

The other two are also experienced in both hardware and software used for communications and connecting devices.

Apple does not stick rigidly to an annual staff review, though, with its most recent appointments and changes taking place immediately after John Ternus took over as CEO in September. In a similar move, Steve Smith was promoted from an assistant role to lead Apple's mergers team after its previous leader retired.

items.title: YouTubers break the iPhone Duo, but stores aren't seeing broken displays
items.content_html:
A YouTuber has demonstrated the resilience of the iPhone Duo display, which seems to explain why there are so few reports of broken units just after launch.

There are some inevitabilities that happen after the launch of a new Apple product. We have seen the initial reviewers' opinions, as well as a close examination of mechanisms, but now we have turned to the destruction phase of the iPhone Duo release.

Released early on Saturday, the video by JerryRigEverything looks at the iPhone Duo and then destroys it in various ways within a few minutes. However, unlike others that sensationalize the destruction for clicks, the channel instead takes a fairly structured and measured approach.

In a scratch test through the Mohs Hardness Scale, the Ceramic Shield-protected front display manages to reach level seven. That's just below the level 8 or 9 of sapphire.

The same cannot be said about the flexible inner display, which does scratch at a level two implement, forming deeper grooves with a fingernail. This is similar to practically all other foldable devices on the market, so Apple isn't alone here.

That said, its multi-level approach with a matte nano-texture finish does help hide any scratches while turned on. Keys, coins, and chain mail armor do leave marks, but they practically disappear when the screen is turned on.

The rest of the video devolves into a series of tests that reveal obvious things. Using a knife on the titanium edge will scratch it, while using a lighter will singe and mark the internal display.

Pouring a massive amount of dirt and dust then opening and closing it does eventually result in a clogged hinge that won't allow it to stay closed. The lesson here is not to bury the iPhone Duo in the sand on a trip to the beach.

As a reminder, quartz sand is 7 on the Mohs scale of hardness, generally harder than glass.

Eventually, a bend test is conducted, trying to "close" the iPhone Duo the wrong way with the large screen on the external side. After exerting a lot of pressure with the thumbs, and some disconcerting cracking sounds, the iPhone Duo does survive, albeit after flexing quite a lot.

The screen did develop a line fault on one side after the first attempt, with more developing after a second attempt. The hinge does allow enough flex for the display to get damaged, but ultimately it doesn't allow the screen to fully snap the iPhone in half.

The video shows that, with enough effort and disregard for financial matters, you can damage an iPhone Duo, which isn't really a thing anyone needed to learn. However, the amount of effort required to seriously damage the internal display without breaking the central creased section nor the hinge shows that it's not as fragile as people may think.

That middle section is still the most vulnerable part, and consumers are also finding that out live.

Posts to the iPhone Duo subreddit show users complaining of cracked screens happening a short time after picking up their devices. In most of the instances, there is a definite central fold and screen issues from the center to the edge.

While alarming in isolation, it's also something that's happening at a far lower rate than people may think. Posts to social media of broken iPhones are always alarming, but it doesn't show how widespread a problem is.

There is always some form of infant failures in Apple product releases, simply because of the sheer number of sales. But even then, it seems to be quite low for the iPhone Duo.

AppleInsider called sources we have worked with for over 15 years that work inside Apple Genius bars at seven stores, including four major flagships. None of the stores polled have seen any devices in for service or returned because of broken screens.

While the worries are understandable, and if it bleeds it leads, especially on social media, the reality is that the iPhone Duo is more formidable than you'd think.

Except if you want to record a YouTube video destroying one.

items.title: OLED upgrades for iMac, MacBook Air are planned but still far from launch
items.content_html:
OLED displays are still planned for the iMac and MacBook Air, but don't expect either upgrade to arrive in the near future.

Apple's "Pro and Tell" special event is forecast to feature the OLED upgrade to the MacBook Pro, among other launches. However, Apple's use of OLED won't stop there, as it still has plans to use it on other less-Pro models.

According to Mark Gurman in Sunday's "Power On" newsletter for Bloomberg, Apple is currently testing new versions of the MacBook Air and iMac. Those prototypes are claimed to include OLED displays.

However, while testing is underway, it doesn't mean there will be a launch of those particular models anytime soon. Gurman says that an updated iMac without OLED is arriving in the coming days, while a new non-OLED MacBook Air will be surfacing early in 2027.

There have been repeated rumors of an OLED update to both lines. However, those rumors have never hinted that an update was imminent for either model.

In December 2025, a supply chain report claimed that a 24-inch iMac update with OLED was arriving in 2027. In August 2026, the OLED iMac was said to arrive in 2029.

For the MacBook Air, analyst Ming-Chi Kuo said in March 2026 that it would be later than expected. While earlier reports claimed a 2027 or 2028 launch was possible, Kuo pointed to it happening in 2029.

It's not the only OLED Mac model that has been rumored about. In September 2026, there was a claim that an OLED MacBook model would be introduced in 2029 to bridge the gap between the MacBook Pro and MacBook Air.

items.title: AI audio firm Samplab acquired by Apple to boost Logic Pro
items.content_html:
Apple has acquired AI audio editing firm Samplab, likely to extend Logic Pro's existing stem splitting tools, as well as adding the ability to edit individual notes in chords.

Following its deal with the Huxe AI podcast company, Apple has now acquired Zurich-based Samplab under a similar arrangement. As detailed in the European Union's public list of acquisitions, Apple is to acquire certain assets, and offer employment to certain Samplab employees.

Samplab was founded in Hauptsitz, Zurich, Switzerland, in 2020 by Manuel Fritsche and Gian-Marco Hutter. It's believed to have no more than 10 employees and based on LinkedIn profiles, may even only employ the two founders.

The company has previously described itself as being about "music production for the age of AI." Before being closed down, its official website promoted how its software could "change any note in your audio," and "detect and edit chords."

Samplab's software also included what the firm described as granular stem separation. Since 2024, Apple's Logic Pro has had stem splitting, which uses AI to isolate vocals, guitars, drums, and so on, into separate tracks.

The company's software was available as a plugin for Digital Audio Workstations (DAW), including Logic Pro. So while neither Samplab nor Apple have commented publicly, it seems most probable that the firm's technology will be used in Apple Creator Studio and Logic Pro.

Samplab's notice to existing users before its website was rerouted to Apple's - image credit: Samplab.

According to the EU, Apple made this deal through an unnamed subsidiary on June 17. In late June, Samplab's official website posted that it was closing down, and would be refunding subscribers with the remainder of their annual subscription fee.

That official site now routes through to apple.com. Other links to Samplab plugins are currently routing to a "page not found" on Apple's site.

Samplab's Twitter channel appears to have been gutted, and its YouTube channel has definitely had its videos removed.

This acquisition is the latest of several reported to the EU, with most being small firms such as Samplab, Huxe, and Prompt AI. It bought Q.Ai in January 2026 for an estimated $2 billion, however, and reportedly may be working to make other large-scale acquisitions.

items.title: Testing iPhone Duo: Apple nearly solved my biggest concerns
items.content_html:
I had three major questions about the form factor of Apple's new iPhone Duo, and wondered if it would work for me. After some time with it, I have my answers.

There are a lot of ways Apple could have approached the first folding iPhone. I've tested a lot of the other popular folding smartphones and while I loved the idea, none had me sold.

While I was debating if I should switch to the iPhone Duo, I had hesitation. My concerns weren't about the crease or battery life.

Instead, I was worried about three things I considered critical: MagSafe, Face ID, and the software.

My MagSafe fears started even before iPhone Duo was announced. A lot of rumors said there would be no MagSafe, which we were skeptical about here at AppleInsider.

Fortunately, those rumors turned out to be wrong. Still, we didn't know how iPhone Duo would work with accessories.

I haven't plugged my iPhone in to charge for years now, so I wanted all my stands to still work. Fortunately, they're mostly fine.

When closed, iPhone Duo perches right onto all the different docks I had. If you place it on horizontally, it goes into StandBy mode.

As we've seen, iPhone Duo will tilt on MagSafe stands when unfolded. Physics are remorseless.

Others issues start to crop up when you move to other accessories, like battery packs and wallets. The phone is just too compact for most of what's out there.

ESR MagSafe wallet with Find My for iPhone Duo

These will all be short-term issues. New accessories are already hitting the market. Moft, ESR, and others have MagSafe wallets that are more compact to fit the Duo's stature.

There are new chargers, too, that hold up the iPhone Duo better while open. So far none of these are shipping yet.

BMX SolidSafe battery for iPhone Duo

Finally, companies have released battery packs that fit the form factor. For instance, the BMX SolidSafe Duo has a built-in stand and display with a 5KmAh capacity that fits right on the back of iPhone Duo.

It even charges wirelessly faster than the similarly-slim iPhone Air, reaching 25W instead of 22W. Even though I may need to buy a new wallet or battery, MagSafe won't be an issue.

The reason I was worried about software was Apple history in neglecting larger screen sizes. With the "pro max" iPhones, Apple doesn't do much more than increase the size of everything on the screen.

The larger iPads have the same issue. There's no good utilization of the 13-inch iPad Pro or iPad Air other than just making things larger and having more space.

Even though I got to try the iPhone Duo at its launch, Apple was still trying to keep some of the experience under wraps until it became available. Since then, I've been thinking about the software and what Apple would need to do to sell me on it.

Vertical StandBy mode for iPhone Duo

In my testing the last few days, I've been focusing on this software. There are certainly areas that could use some polish, but I think Apple exceeded my expectations here.

StandBy mode has been an early favorite. There are new StandBy options like weather with live animations, a new calendar view, and the great Modular face.

Using iPhone Duo in StandBy mode next to my Mac

StandBy mode works not only when placed landscape on a charger, but any time you prop it up. It can be standing or in tent mode and it doesn't need to be plugged in.

It's a solid desktop companion, showing me my news feed, the time, and my calendar. Notifications also slide in elegantly so I don't miss anything.

iPhone Duo can run apps side by side

Split screen apps are flawless. The gesture feels second-nature already to pin apps to the sides and lock them into place.

And then, there's that clever animation when you open and close the phone. I've still not gotten tired of it and I doubt I ever will.

Kid Cue, Dual Display, and Smart Take are incredible camera features. I'm going to be using all of these a lot.

The side-aligned dock is very comfortable to use, but it does stick out a bit on unupdated apps.

When apps get updated, they will support this extra space. Until they do, it'll be very "early iPad" with just larger screens and black bars. It's promising so far, and will only get better.

MagSafe and the software are non-issues, but the lack of Face ID is still going to bother me.

iPhone Duo doesn't have Face ID

Without Face ID, Apple chose to revert to Touch ID instead. So far, my fingers don't always work with Touch ID, so I don't think I could use it full time.

Apple tried to make it easier to use by leveraging a feature first found on the Mac. If you wear an Apple Watch, you can automatically unlock your phone when you swipe.

The Apple Watch must be unlocked and detect the heart rate on your wrist. It also has to be in close proximity to your phone, and when the phone unlocks, it taps your wrist.

Pro tip: if you disable "rest to unlock" it goes faster, too. For me, it's worked reliably.

It's super-fast and most of the time, I forgot I wasn't using Face ID. But there are those times that it unlocks accidentally, like a few times in my pocket.

And, periodically, the phone will require you to unlock with Touch ID instead.

The Touch ID sensor on iPhone Duo

Touch ID as an authentication method feels like a step back, and I think it would be an important addition to the second-generation. That seems probable to us.

If I didn't have an Apple Watch, I'm not sure I'd be able to use iPhone Duo. The lack of Touch ID would bother me that much.

If you get the opportunity to try an iPhone Duo, I'm confident you'll love it. The new foldable feels premium, clever, and is a joy to use.

Just like it did for iPad, Apple will iterate on software and the user interface as it sees how people are using it. That's part of the experience of being an early adopter.

I'm happy that my biggest concerns are largely non-issues, and I'll happily use iPhone Duo as my daily driver. But even if you ignore the price, that doesn't mean the phone is for everyone. Most average users will be happy holding off for a polished second-generation unit, or sticking with the conventional design.

items.title: John Ternus welcomes iPhone Duo line at Austin Apple Store
items.content_html:
Apple's flagship foldable went on sale on Friday, and as is tradition, the Apple CEO was there to kick off the sales.

Crowds flocked around Apple Stores worldwide as the iPhone Duo went on sale. As is tradition, Apple's CEO opened the doors at one of the stores.

This time, though, it wasn't Tim Cook, nor was it in New York City. It was John Ternus, who took over as Apple CEO in September.

Ternus threw open the doors at 9:00 am local time at Apple Domain Northside, located in Austin, Texas. The store first opened in November 2017.

He was joined by Senior Vice President of Retail Deirdre O'Brien.

Generally, the CEO opens the Fifth Avenue location. Instead, that location was opened by Apple's senior vice president of Worldwide Marketing Greg Joswiak and Vice President of Stores and Retail Operations Vanessa Trigub.

Greg Joswiak and Vanessa Trigub welcome visitors to the Apple Fifth Avenue store in New York, where sales of the iPhone Duo will begin.

John Ternus is, unexpectedly, not there. Instead, the head of Apple's global marketing and the head of the company's retail stores are present. https://t.co/oQxfrzHX9D

Apple opened preorders for the iPhone Duo on October 16. On Friday, October 23, the iPhone Duo finally began making its way into customers' hands.

items.title: The iPhone Duo finally makes its way into customers' hands
items.content_html:
iPhone Duo preorders are showing up at customers' doorsteps ad in Apple Stores as Apple's first foldable rolls out worldwide.

Apple opened preorders for the iPhone Duo on October 16 ahead of its October 23 release date. It didn't take long for release dates to slip and eventually stabilize in mid-January.

Deliveries typically begin in Australia and New Zealand, then Asia, Europe, and North America. Apple Stores generally open at 8:00 AM local time to cater to launch-day enthusiasts.

Launch day crowds in Apple Jing'an Shanghai - image credit: Apple

Early recipients have taken to social media to post photos and first impressions of the new devices. These posts also offer customers elsewhere an early look at the device before their own deliveries arrive.

Line outside Apple Fifth Avenue around 4:15 AM for iPhone Duo https://t.co/nqpuc3qo41

Demonstrating the new iPhone Duo to customers at Apple Jing'an - image credit: Apple

Despite expectation that iPhone Duo stocks in store would be low to even none, and Apple specifically saying that they are limited, crowds have gathered at stores worldwide.

The very first customer at Apple Jing'an - image credit: Apple.

Apple Store staff were cautious about stock levels first thing, not being willing to confirm how many in a queue would get one.

As well as pre-orders arriving, Apple Stores have added display models. This is Apple Birmingham in the UK.

Customers in the U.S. will begin receiving their preorders on Friday morning as delivery services start their routes. Apple Stores will also have limited numbers of the iPhone Duo available for in-store pickup and walk-in purchases.

items.title: Apple Music has hidden a classic & interactive iPod online
items.content_html:
Apple Music is still celebrating the iPod, although only if you know exactly where to look. Here's where to find it.

On October 23, 2026, the iPhone Duo shipped, but 25 years earlier, to the day, Steve Jobs announced the iPod. It's been a remarkable road from one device to the other, but even as the spotlight is on the iPhone Duo, Apple has launched an almost fully working virtual iPod.

"Launched" is possibly not the right word, as you have to either know where to look, or manage to get Apple Music to return an error message. That's where this iPod is, it is hidden on the Apple Music online site.

So not the app, but the online version. It's the one for Apple Music subscribers who are stuck on PCs at work.

To go have a look on an iPhone or iPad, long-press on this address, https://music.apple.com/404 and choose Open. Be sure not to choose Open in Music, as that simply takes you to the Apple Music app.

You can press and hold on that URL to see a preview. That's also possible on macOS, but to get the full-size iPod on a Mac, right-click on the link and choose Open.

Maybe Apple has always had a virtual iPod that it made for Steve Jobs (right) - image credit: Apple.

What you now get is a typical web 404 page, except alongside the usual "page not found" message, it says "Give this a spin instead." The text, written in Apple's old favorite font Garamond, is next to an image of an iPod.

It's gorgeous. Plus in every way bar one, it even works like an old iPod.

So you have a click wheel and you can scroll through settings or music. And such a lot of music, probably getting on for 1,000 tracks.

You can scroll to choose any of them, and as you scroll, you hear the once-famous, now forgotten, but so very welcome click. The iPod clicks as you scroll, and then you can press on its center button to select and play a track.

It is so thoroughly lifelike that if you select a song, it will appear to play it. So you get a progress bar through the song.

The only thing AppleInsider couldn't make it do was have that track be audible. Doubtlessly every song is in Apple Music, but perhaps the rights don't include letting it be played where you don't have to be a subscriber.

It's not as if many people are going to stumble across it, though. This is an error page and realistically you're only ever going to find it if someone tells you.

So thank you Edward Munn, whose blog reported it first.

To be fair, neither he nor we can be certain that this error page was added specifically for this 25th anniversary of the iPod. Maybe it's been this way for a long time, but just in case and also just in case it goes away, do be sure to try it out now.

Funny. When Apple killed off the last iPod, it did so with a press release that rankled because it was trying to make it sound like a good thing. "The music lives on," it said.

But 25 years after the launch of the iPod and four years since it died, maybe Apple had a point.

items.title: iPod changed the world a quarter of a century ago
items.content_html:
One day the iPod was everywhere and the next it was nowhere. But this device that propelled Apple toward the iPhone may never be forgotten.

It surprised the world that Apple, of all companies, was the one to produce a hit music player when so many others had failed. But then it absolutely shocked the world when Apple itself killed it off.

In retrospect, the iPod was a light bulb product. Suddenly it was switched on and it was everywhere, but then just as suddenly it was switched off and gone forever.

Or nearly forever. It's now a quarter of a century since it was first announced on October 23, 2001 and from when it first appeared in stores on November 10 that year. All these years on, the iPod is gone yet seemingly never forgotten.

You may be among the (literally) millions of people who remember it fondly. Or you might be among the brave few trying to relaunch it in the hope that Apple won't notice.

Either way, the iPod was enormously successful, enormously popular, it changed the world in so many ways, and then it vanished.

Or at least the device itself did. A quarter of a century on, we have the podcast industry that the iPod created, and named.

As we say, it wouldn't actually ship until November 10, 2001, but on October 23 of that year, Steve Jobs talked to press in what now seems like such a small room.

"We lured you here today," he told them, "with the promise of unveiling a breakthrough digital device that's not a Mac."

Subscribe to AppleInsider on YouTube

Jobs did then hype up the Mac during his typical scene-setting before the real unveiling. In this case, at this time, he argued that the Mac could be the center of people's lives, working with their other devices.

It's a very odd presentation to look back on because the opening ten minutes or so have Steve Jobs talking up and then demonstrating Apple's iWork apps like iTunes and iMovie.

Even back then, these were known, none of this was new. And there's a sense of patient waiting from the room.

And then Jobs makes the pitch they've come for, the pitch that would show how Apple was going to take on all of the existing MP3 players. "As we've been designing these apps, of course we've been paying a lot of attention to the devices," said Jobs. "We want it to work with all of the coolest devices and we have to learn everything about these devices to make our iApps work."

"So the iApps know all about these devices, but the thought occurred to us late last year that the devices don't know anything the iApps," he continued. "There's never been a device that's been built that can take advantage of all this amazing intelligence built into these apps running on a Mac."

Jobs had actually built up to announcing a music player in such a way that he could even have taken a left turn and revealed a camera. He was pushing Apple as the answer to everything, and saying it was starting with music because "we love music."

But there was a practical side to this, and it was to do with how big a market music is. "Music's been around forever, it will always be around," said Jobs, "[so this] is not a speculative market."

Calling a global market, Jobs made the case that everyone was then living through a digital music revolution, and yet there was a problem. There was no market leader, and even large firms like Sony "haven't had a hit yet."

Steve Jobs claimed that Apple had found the recipe to making the best music player, the best audio product. "And that product is called iPod," he said.

Which ones did you have?

No reaction. Jobs was delivering this speech with the same precision as for the iPhone and iPad launches, and with the same persuasive reality-distorting tone. But the small audience was not whooping or cheering.

Perhaps that was because iPod didn't immediately mean anything, where it would later be obvious what iPhone meant. Reportedly, Apple chose the name because the prototype somehow reminded copywriter Vinnie Chieco of the famous line "Open the pod bay doors, Hal," from "2001: A Space Odyssey."

If the audience was cold to the name, they warmed up, though, as Jobs turned to specifications, and most especially because he claimed that the iPod held 1,000 songs — and held them in your pocket. He talked about the tiny hard drive, he talked compression rates, and he also talked about FireWire.

Now long-abandoned, FireWire was a dramatically faster way of transferring data between devices than previously. Jobs spelt it out, too. He said that it takes five to ten seconds to load a CD's music onto an iPod using FireWire.

And then he compared iPod to the then-current USB (not USB-C) music players. "On a USB player, you're talking five minutes."

To put all 1,000 songs onto the iPod, it was under 10 minutes. "On a USB player... you get to watch it for five hours while it loads the songs."

Those specifications in full were:

That $399 in 2001 is the equivalent of around $760 in 2026, so this was far from a cheap device.

But it worked. You could pick it up and immediately know how to play music, and how to find particular tracks or artists.

It perhaps took a little bit of reading the manual to know how to connect your iPod to your Mac, or then to Windows.

But compared to how fiddly most other MP3 players had been, the iPod was the right device at the right time. Even if it still took a couple of years before it became the ubiquitous device that it did.

Depending on how you counted it — whether you include spec bump updates or not — there were eventually around 28 models of iPod. Those broke down into categories:

As well as eventually issuing an iPod photo, Apple would add a version of the iPod with video.

Just a sample of the many different iPod models Apple made.

Not all of these models were a hit, but most were. Possibly the only one to get generally poor reviews was the iPod shuffle, but that still had four generations from 2005 to 2010.

The iPod shuffle was the only iPod without a screen and the idea was that you just let it play rather than trying to find particular tracks.

If that one was comparatively a flop, the idea of the iPod was such a hit that it is yet another product that transformed Apple. The iMac saved it from bankruptcy and the iPhone set it on the road to trillions of dollars, but the iPod played a part.

It was the iPod that showed Apple was a consumer electronics firm rather than a solely computer one. It was arguably one element that also helped Apple gain a reputation for being late to a market, yet then transforming it.

Make no mistake, either, the iPod was transformative. If it's surprising that previous music players were comparatively poor, though, it's got to be even more surprising how rivals failed to follow Apple's lead in usability.

Microsoft tried, but even it took five years more to produce its Zune music player. This was back when Microsoft would do things like creating marketing terms such as "Plays For Sure," but not actually have its Zune play much at all.

That attempt to beat the iPod took half a decade to come out, and then Microsoft killed it after another half a decade. That Zune was such a flop that you may not have even noticed it was gone.

But then the iPod was a startling success and yet you may not know when that ended. If you've noticed that no one has iPods anymore or that Apple doesn't sell them, you might still be surprised to learn that the end came in 2022.

May 2022 was when the last iPod was discontinued, and this iPod touch then remained on sale only until stocks ran out. It was a very quiet ending to such a worldwide runaway hit.

Except May 2022 was more like the eventual turning off life support when the device was already long gone. Six years after Steve Jobs's rather low-key, small-scale presentation of the iPod, Apple announced the iPhone.

It wasn't just the headline, Apple's announcement of the end of the iPod was all upbeat about how great Apple Music was instead - image credit: Apple.

Specifically because of how successful the iPod had been, that Steve Jobs presentation was more how we remember them all. His style was the same, his way of building up to a point was the same, but now he was doing it in front of a large and very enthusiastic audience.

Today that presentation is an easier watch than the iPod one because it's slick and if iPhone features have changed, they've really just developed. Seeing how they started is fascinating.

It was at the time, too, but a key difference between then and now is how Steve Jobs really had to include one thing in his sales pitch. He had to tell the audience that Apple was launching what he described as a "widescreen iPod with touch controls."

The fact that the new device was a phone was ultimately the key thing, but right at that moment, iPod was so hot that it had to be namechecked. It was a selling point.

Perhaps you could have predicted that the iPhone would make the iPod obsolete, and certainly Apple did. Apple reasoned that it was better for them to make an iPod killer than wait for a rival to do it.

Naturally, Apple wouldn't say that aloud then or now, and shortly after the iPhone launched, it brought out the iPod touch.

Only, where the iPhone had to be called a type of iPod, at least once, things changed even by September 2006 when the iPod touch was announced. By the time it was, it was seen as an iPhone without the phone.

The torch might still have been blazing, but it had been passed on.

If you still have a working iPod, you may now be able to update it and even work with AirPods. Sprout Pi Mainboard is a crowdfunding project that promises to bring your iPod into the 2020s.

Search eBay for "iPod" and that's the rest of your day taken up as you go through hundreds of listings. The volume of them is partly because there were so many versions, partly because so many were sold, but also because they're popular and they sell.

Some listings say that their iPods have new batteries in them. But at the very least, you're buying a used device that is four years old, and potentially 25 years old.

So maybe you can't expect them to perform as they did, to have the battery life that they once had. And if it's really just the music you're buying for, then an iPhone will do that and more.

It's likely, though, that iPods are being bought as much for nostalgia as for audio quality. And people's memories of this device are so strong that some companies and individuals have tried to take advantage.

So in 2025, a 3D modeller launched the iFidget. It looks like an iPod and it has familiar scroll wheel, but it doesn't play music.

The iFidget solely exists to bring back memories of the clicking sound when you rotated that wheel to make a selection.

It might not be playing music, but it is very definitely designed like an iPod. Then in October 2026, a startup called New Matter announced the Sudo music player, and you already know what it looks like.

Sudo's new iPod-like music player

That's not the first iPod clone and it won't be the last. But whether firms do this out of love or just want to make cash from people who do love the iPod, there is plenty of affection going around.

A quarter of a century after it launched, and four years since Apple stopped making it, the iPod still has its fans.

items.title: Appeals court upholds Apple TV's 'Servant' plagiarism lawsuit win
items.content_html:
There's no twist ending for M. Nigh Shyamalan's day in court, as the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals has maintained the ruling that Apple TV's "Servant" series did not copy a film titled "The Truth About Emanuel."

A lawsuit brought on by filmmaker Francesca Gregorini in January 2020 accused the creators of Servant of plagiarizing her film. The case was initially dismissed, but was then brought back to trial by jury, which ruled in favor of Apple.

Gregorini appealed the decision, but according to a report from Reuters, the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals rejected the challenge. While both The Truth About Emanuel and Servant are both about a mother grieving the death of their child and becoming attached to a doll, that's where the similarities end.

The jury determined as much after viewing both the film and the first three episodes of the Apple TV series. M. Night Shyamalan said during court before the original ruling that there was "clearly, 100% a misunderstanding."

Servant aired its final season in March 2023, but the entire series is still available to watch on Apple TV. If you've yet to watch the thrilling series, now is the perfect time to pick it up right before Halloween.

items.title: Critical PHP vulnerabilities threaten your NAS, not every vendor has a fix
items.content_html:
Attackers are actively exploiting critical PHP flaws to target internet-exposed NAS devices. If your files and backups are stored there, they're probably at risk.

PHP2Shell refers to two critical vulnerabilities in PHP, a scripting language used by web servers and some NAS services. The flaws, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, could allow attackers to execute code on affected servers without logging in.

The PHP development team released security updates on October 21 for versions 8.2 through 8.5. The urgency isn't hypothetical, as Amazon detected an attempted exploit on October 17, four days before the vulnerabilities were publicly disclosed.

For NAS owners, the threat affects both software maintained by the manufacturer and applications running independently in Docker containers. In either case, the risk of a remote attack depends on whether attackers can reach the vulnerable PHP service.

Synology has released updated PHP packages addressing the vulnerabilities. Its security advisory identifies PHP versions 7.3 through 8.4, Mail Station, and Synology Calendar among the affected products.

Updated PHP 8.2 and PHP 8.4 packages are available through Synology's Package Center and download archive. Owners should check the advisory for the status of other affected packages rather than assume every component has been patched.

Synology also distinguishes separately installed PHP packages from the PHP components built into DiskStation Manager. The manufacturer says its built-in PHP isn't exposed to external attack surfaces, making exploitation through that component unlikely.

QNAP confirmed a wider range of affected products in its October 22 advisory. The list includes QTS 5.2.11 and earlier, QTS 6.1.0, multiple versions of QuTS hero and QuTScloud, and applications such as Note Station 3.

The company is working on fixes but hasn't said when they will be available. QNAP reports no attacks targeting its products, though attempts to exploit vulnerable PHP servers have been documented.

Until patches arrive, QNAP recommends removing direct internet exposure by disabling unnecessary port forwarding, UPnP, and remote-access services. Owners who need remote connections should use a VPN and restrict management access to trusted networks.

Disabling the built-in web server can reduce exposure if the service isn't needed, but QNAP warns that doing so doesn't protect the NAS administration interface. Network restrictions remain necessary while the affected software is unpatched.

TerraMaster has acknowledged the problem in a Reddit discussion after an owner reported finding PHP 7.4.33 running the management interface on an F2-425 NAS.

In an October 22 response, TerraMaster said its team was investigating and testing the issue and working toward a fix. We haven't independently confirmed that the reported configuration is exploitable, and there is not yet a patch.

We also haven't been able to confirm whether Ugreen has released a PHP2Shell security update for UGOS Pro. The company's vulnerability policy describes how it handles security reports, but doesn't establish whether its NAS software is affected by these vulnerabilities.

Similarly, we couldn't confirm a PHP2Shell patch or a definitive affected-device list from Asustor. The manufacturer maintains a security advisory page, although the status of the specific vulnerability is listed as "ongoing."

NAS owners should check their manufacturer's security notices and available updates for their specific models.

Even a fully updated NAS operating system may still be running vulnerable PHP software inside Docker containers. These applications can include their own PHP installations, which aren't necessarily updated when the manufacturer patches the NAS firmware.

Owners running PHP-based services in Docker should check their container images for affected versions and install updated images as they become available. Applying an image update generally requires recreating the container so it runs the patched software.

QNAP explicitly warns that PHP installations inside Container Station and third-party applications aren't covered by its operating-system updates. The Dutch National Cyber Security Center also recommends identifying PHP installations in third-party software and applying the appropriate fixes.

If an affected container can't be updated immediately, owners should disable public access or restrict connections until a patch arrives. These measures reduce the risk of remote attacks but can't replace the security fixes recommended by PHP developers.

The greatest long-term concern involves older NAS hardware that no longer gets security updates. When manufacturer support ends, vulnerabilities can remain unpatched indefinitely, leaving owners exposed to known security problems beyond PHP2Shell.

An unsupported NAS can still provide local file storage, but exposing its administrative interface or other services directly to the internet creates unnecessary risk. Owners should remove public access rather than assume older hardware will eventually receive a fix.

Blocking unsolicited inbound connections keeps the device accessible locally while allowing outbound traffic for updates and other services.

For remote access, owners should use a secure VPN instead of forwarding NAS management ports. They should also check logs for suspicious activity, since updates won't undo an existing compromise.

items.title: Inside the iPhone Duo's groundbreaking hinge's innovations
items.content_html:
A YouTuber has taken a CT scan of the hinge on the iPhone Duo and uncovered both how it works and what its limitations are.

One of the surprises at the iPhone Duo launch was how it wasn't just built to either be fully open or fully closed. Instead, Apple has built it to offer different functions at many different angles.

According to testing done by HTX Studio on YouTube, iPhone Duo can stay open between 15 degrees and 145 degrees. If it's held below 15 degrees, magnets mean it will snap shut. Similarly, beyond 145 degrees, the screen will snap to fully open.

Apple has already said that its hinge contains almost 100 components. A CT scan of the hinge shows that this is concentrated in six sections, including two at the outer edges that are hinges connected to a central shaft.

Another section is a series of gears that are made so that rotating one side of the device also rotates the other. They stay in sync, they stay in lockstep, practically regardless of where you hold them.

Key to the design are two more sections immediately above and below the middle. These are a mix of springs and cams that either support or resist one another, depending on the angle of the screen.

"When the phone is fully open, the cams fit together, while the springs press against them to resist rotation, holding the foam until we apply enough force to fold it," says HTX Studio's video. "As we fold it, the cams compress the springs, which push back, and the resulting frictional torque overcomes the phone's own weight."

All of these sections are paired, with the same mechanical design at the top and bottom of the hinge. The final section is in the center, and seemingly features no moving parts.

Instead, it's the space through which flex cables connecting the two sides of the iPhone Duo can pass uninterrupted.

It's already been demonstrated by Apple that the iPhone Duo screen hides the crease in part through the ten layers of glass on the display. Plus it has a nanotexture display where all other foldables have glossy ones, meaning they practically highlight the crease in comparison.

But beyond that, this new CT scan also reveals the details of one hinge element where Apple does much the same as its rivals.

The top and bottom of the iPhone Duo hinge are mirror images of each other - image credit HTX Studio.

It's called the bending space and represents what radius the curved screen goes to.

"Think of the screen as a sheet of paper," says the video. "Fold it in half with a wide curve, and there won't be much of a crease when you open it, but press it flat with no room to bend, and you will get a very clear crease."

On the iPhone Duo, this bending space is 3.85mm at its widest point. That lies between the 3.8mm and 4.2mm of other unspecified but typical foldables.

Apple has achieved an IP68 rating for dust resistance, which is rare for a foldable, but still no reason to throw yours down on a beach. Nonetheless, it is something few rivals can match.

Similarly, most rivals reportedly have the same two small bumps at top and bottom of the crease that are there to protect their hinges. If dropped, such foldables can disperse the jolt to the metal sides of the phone instead of into the screen.

Apple's iPhone Duo does not have this and instead, the screen gets to be perfectly smooth all over. It's also able to do this because the entire hinge assembly is encased in a titanium cover for extra strength.

The iPhone Duo can support an Apple Pencil, but doing so means writing on the device's surface with a fairly hard-tipped device. HTX Studio, though, tested out not only an Apple Pencil but also regular pencils from 6B to 8H hardness, and tried them in a rig pressing down with a force of 100g.

There was a faintly visible mark on the display with a 6H pencil, but it wasn't apparent to the touch. At 8H, there were much more visible and touchable scratches.

But reportedly this is better than many rival foldables.

The video goes into more detail about the design and components that the CT scan revealed. The YouTubers did this on a review model, and, separately, other reviewers have put theirs through more real-world tests.

items.title: Intelligent Assistant added to iWork apps for Creative Studio subscribers
items.content_html:
Apple added a beta Intelligent Assistant to Pages, Keynote, and Numbers on Thursday, but only Apple Creator Studio subscribers get it.

On Thursday, Apple updated its iWork trio of apps: the word processor Pages, the presentation app Keynote, and the spreadsheet app Numbers. The update added support for the iPhone Duo, set to reach customers starting October 23.

According to Apple, there's also a new Interchange Format (.keyx). Because the format is open, it should make editing Keynote files in other apps easier.

The brunt of the update has been reserved for Apple Intelligence features. These features are paywalled behind Apple Creator Studio, Apple's creative software subscription bundle.

All three apps are getting a new beta Intelligent Assistant. To use it, you'll need to have your device set to US English and updated to iOS 27 or later.

As 9to5Mac notes, this assistant appears to be separate from Siri AI. Here's what it's capable of, according to Apple:

Pages

Keynote

Numbers

Apple issued the updates on Thursday afternoon. Shortly after release, Apple pulled all three apps from both the iOS and Mac App Store. It is unknown if this is a bug or intentional.

items.title: iPhone Duo buyers line up days early despite high chance of heartbreak
items.content_html:
Apple's first foldable iPhone is drawing buyers to storefronts days before launch, while the first preorders are shipping for Friday delivery.

People are already lining up at Apple Stores across the globe, hoping for a chance at getting an iPhone Duo. Unfortunately, limited stock means many hopeful buyers will not be leaving with a new device.

Apple never shares firm production numbers, especially before a product is released. However, Apple has said there will be limited stock at retail available on Friday.

That warning hasn't stopped people from lining up, though. Lexus C on X shared a short video of Apple Galaxy Macau, where hundreds of people have lined up two days in advance.

As we approach iPhone Duo launch day, people around the world have started lining up outside Apple Stores! This is Apple Galaxy Macau. We're still 48 hours from launch time, but there's already a huge crowd. https://t.co/EcWA7ZB9iy

He also shared snapshots of the Apple Firth Ave store, where people began arriving 30 hours before the device was set to go on sale.

(reported by @JurgenMeco and @ mgcf1) As we approach the 30-hour countdown, the walk-in line for iPhone Duo at Apple Fifth Ave currently has around 5-6 people waiting. And the staff has been working on the giant iPhone Duo models at the storefront! https://t.co/AoMDraTjjl

TechDroider on Facebook also showed early lines forming at stores.

If you've got a preorder, you're going to start getting shipment notifications on Thursday if you haven't already. Some buyers are also reporting that Apple has shipped out their iPhone Duo, with October 23 delivery dates.

iPhone Duo: Shipped! https://t.co/RXEUQaONzq

The iPhone Duo was announced at Apple's "Surprise and Shine" event on September 9. Apple's first foldable starts at $1,999 for the base model; despite that high price tag, it sold out within minutes.

Wait times for shipments from Apple have stretched into January 2027.

items.title: iPhone Duo 2 will have under-display Face ID
items.content_html:
A new report claims that not only is Apple aiming to add Face ID to a future iPhone Duo, but that it may not need a notch or cutout.

While the first iPhone Duo appears to be something of a hit, it is lacking the key Face ID feature from other iPhones. It would be startling if Apple weren't working to add this, but according to Bloomberg, it's coming.

Specifically, it will come as soon as the next generation of the iPhone Duo. It is to be Face ID as we know it, but the sensor will be under the display.

Apple is believed to have been working on under-display Face ID for some time. The current iPhone Duo actually features Apple's first-ever under-display camera system, so it seems feasible that Face ID could be next.

That under-display camera in the opened-out iPhone Duo, though, means that the device has two selfie cameras. So regardless of whether the iPhone Duo is open or closed, users can make video FaceTime calls.

However, speaking on his "Power On" podcast, Bloomberg writer Mark Gurman claims that iPhone Duo 2 will solely have Face ID on its front screen.

Reportedly versions of the iPhone Duo 2 are already being tested internally at Apple. It's not clear, though, whether those will feature Face ID, as the report also claims that Apple is experimenting with bringing back the Action Button.

This was the one exterior control that was removed from the iPhone Duo and it is hard to see where there would be space to feature it. Nonetheless, even though it appeared to be the end of the Action Button, Apple is reportedly at least considering its return.

items.title: Apple Vision Pro with M5 review one year later: Signs of life in a platform on hold
items.content_html:
After a year of use, it remains clear that the Apple Vision Pro benefits from the power of M5, even if not much else changed. Apple's work is far from over.

I'm writing this review with ten Safari tabs open in a carousel, Drafts below, Music in a mini player on my right, and various social apps behind me. The Apple Vision Pro with M5 isn't showing signs of strain, and that's even with visionOS 27 running as I write some portions of this review.

It shouldn't be. It's M5 after all.

Anyway. The Apple Vision Pro is a complicated device to discuss.

It still feels magical every time I put it on, but the software other than the OS is nearly identical to where it was one or even two years ago.

Apple Vision Pro continues to be an amazing piece of technology three years after its reveal during WWDC 2023, and one year into M5, everything feels new again.

Neglect from developers and Apple itself has left Apple Vision Pro in a software quagmire. Since my previous review, Apple Creator Studio came and went with no apps for Apple Vision Pro, no iPad-compatible apps offered by Apple have become native, and the only new app is the Siri AI app introduced with visionOS 27.

Apple Vision Pro review: still a great productivity tool

Layoffs have impacted Apple Vision Pro's gaming and immersive video teams, and there are no signs of release pacing for either product increasing. It's all on external studios and developers to keep pushing out Vision Pro-specific content, and there's just no money in it.

To top it all off, the Apple Vision Pro is now even more expensive at $3,699 thanks to AI-driven RAM shortages.

To any outside observer reading those preceding paragraphs, things look bleak for Apple Vision Pro. Matters are even more dire when you account for the fact that new Apple CEO John Ternus is allegedly not a fan of the product.

Apple Vision Pro review: the Dual Knit band might be enough to help some people be comfortable

All that said, I don't think Apple has given up on the Apple Vision Pro just yet. It's still selling in some limited fashion, the users that love it do love it a lot, and new apps are being built, if slowly.

This review might look a little different from my other Apple Vision Pro reviews. So much ink has already been spilled on these subjects, and given the stagnant nature of the platform, there isn't much to add. Unfortunately.

So, one year after the Apple Vision Pro M5 release, let's get into the state of it in late 2026.

We've already highlighted the state of the platform from a wider corporate view, many times, so let's get into the hardware itself. As it stands in late 2026, my opinion hasn't wavered — Apple Vision Pro is unmatched.

Apple Vision Pro review: no competing headset comes close

But wait, I just spent several paragraphs basically spelling out the epitaph of Apple's expensive headset. Sure, that is a reality we have to face for the platform today, but none of that affects how Apple Vision Pro works or feels.

Apple Vision Pro has been an accomplishment in the market, and you can tell just by looking at the competition. Android XR, Meta Quest, and others have pursued visionOS-like layouts, gestures, and features since Apple's headset hit the market.

None of them come close to the fidelity provided by Apple Vision Pro. They're all pursuing it on lesser hardware, and some come close, but they can't quite get there without significantly increasing the price of the hardware itself.

Some have suggested that this means Apple should have made a headset with lower specs and a lower price tag. However, this ignores the fact that the headset market itself is quite limited as it is, and another in the competing sub $1,000 price bracket would be virtually ignored.

The M5 version didn't change much. It swapped out the M2 for the M5 and introduced the new Dual Knit band.

The M5 is noticeably more powerful given it can drive the full resolution of the included displays at a higher refresh rate. Widgets aren't left in a blank state as you turn your head as often, and apps don't crash in the background either.

The Dual Knit band helps make the weight of the Apple Vision Pro mostly ignorable for me. I can wear it for hours at a time without needing a break for neck fatigue, though my eyes do need a rest from time to time like with any display.

Apple Vision Pro review: if Apple's bands don't work, try a third-party option

I never had an issue with the Solo Knit band and didn't like the Dual Loop band for the original Apple Vision Pro. I've tested the ResMed and CMA1 alternative bands, and each offered their own ways to manage the Apple Vision Pro's weight.

Counterweights only increased the total weight load on your head and neck, and alternative pads helped with weight distribution, but never felt overly premium. They helped some folks find a good fit, but they never worked for me.

The Dual Knit band ended up being the perfect solution. It has such a wide surface area that I'm almost wearing a helmet. The top strap keeps the Apple Vision Pro basically suspended above my nose while the rear band keeps the pressure distributed around my temples.

Of course, everyone's fit and comfort will be different. You'll have to find what works for you.

Thankfully, the software needed to do my job has been there since the start. I write in Drafts, I research and publish in Safari, and I use Indigo and Tapestry for watching for new stories.

Apple Vision Pro review: a new Safari tab view in visionOS 27

I do wish more of these apps were native Apple Vision Pro ones, but the iPad-compatible versions are good enough. Placing the windows and widgets around my office still feels fun and whimsical in a way even iPad can't match.

The Apple Vision Pro continues to be the best place to view almost any kind of media. It elevates simple still photos, adds depth to panoramas, and makes every video into a movie theater.

My collection of 3D movies in the Apple TV keeps growing, and Apple Immersive Video gets new content from time to time. Apple's work in the sports industry has even brought some interesting features to life, like watching an NBA or MLB game live in immersive.

I guess Apple Vision Pro might be the only place outside of theaters to watch The Odyssey in the glorious IMAX format. It would be a waste if Apple doesn't find a way to make it happen.

Apple Vision Pro review: watching MLB games in immersive format is amazing

Of course, I mean this should be present in the Apple TV app as a version purchasable from the Apple TV Store. There is an IMAX app on Apple Vision Pro, but it's essentially dead, and I'd prefer not have a purchased movie siloed there anyway.

It's easy to look at the snail's pace progress of Apple Vision Pro and get frustrated. It's an expensive piece of hardware that's seen very little budge in the past few years.

However, as Tim Cook said, Apple knew Vision Pro would be for a niche audience that wanted to glimpse the future of computing. No one knows Apple's success targets for the platform or what things look like as it moves forward.

Apple is a weird company inside and out. It doesn't operate like other companies, so trying to apply the same logic to Apple that you might other companies doesn't always work.

Apple Vision Pro might be on its way out for all we know, but there are enough signs to suggest otherwise. It's quite possibly the worst the platform will ever be, and that's saying something considering how great it is today.

As good as the hardware is, I can't ignore the state of things in software. This isn't a review of visionOS, you've already got that from me this year.

When I say software, I mean the app ecosystem. Imagine if iPad didn't get a notable new app in a year. That is essentially where we are with Apple Vision Pro, minus some vibecoded software that mostly needs to be sideloaded.

Don't get me wrong, there are new apps for Apple Vision Pro, and some even appear interesting. Some of the very few new games are interesting, but none capture my attention long.

Gaming on Apple Vision Pro is precisely where I left it a year ago. Thrasher got a remastered update with PSVR2 support and better visuals, but that's the only one that seems to have done such an update.

Apple Vision Pro review: gaming has barely budged in a year

Most of the games on my Apple Vision Pro have no update history or updates from two years ago. The few that do show recent updates within a few months are bug fixes or basic changes.

Apple Arcade might be the only place gaming actually exists on Apple Vision Pro, and given the layoffs, that may soon stop. Developers will have to bring games to Apple Vision Pro on their own, and I don't see an incentive to do so.

The other side of this is game streaming. Whether it's via NVIDIA GeForce Now or a custom-built PC, streaming VR to Apple Vision Pro is one of the best ways on the market to interact with that content.

Apple Vision Pro review: a great gaming companion even without many games on the platform

Sure, Apple Vision Pro is heavy, but for flight simulators like X-Plane 12, it's perfect for immersion. Developers can even develop special controllers that remain visible when fully immersed and track to game environments.

Those with an expensive iRacing rig can also take advantage of the high resolution and frame rates offered by Apple Vision Pro. iVRY is another option for those that already have a VR gaming library on a capable Windows gaming PC.

The app situation isn't much better. I browse the Apple Vision Pro App Store from time to time to find very little has changed.

Apple Vision Pro review: productivity apps haven't budged in a year

Apple's editors almost never write new "Today" stories or roundups. Very few apps are for productivity, instead several focus on single-use experiences like viewing objects in space.

It's not that those kinds of apps aren't welcome, but they hardly help make Apple Vision Pro more viable as a platform. What's worse is Apple's total absence from the story.

I still can't edit photos on Apple Vision Pro without a third-party app or Mac Virtual Display. While I love that I can bring my Mac into the virtual view, it's more of an escape hatch than anything.

Apple Vision Pro review: Siri AI is useful but not a productivity suite

There are also some odd decisions in Apple Vision Pro I still don't understand. Find My doesn't exist in any form, locking windows doesn't matter if you accidentally invoke the app elsewhere, and keyboards still disappear when fully immersed unless you buy Apple's.

It's a weird platform with plenty of quirks and rough edges to smooth out, but even then, it's industry-leading. Every new OS brings new ideas, bug fixes, and streamlined features.

I'll chalk most of this up to growing pains as Apple prepares for what's next in spatial computing. None of this means Apple Vision Pro is bad or dead, nor does it mean Apple has abandoned the product.

It's a weird time to be a fan of Apple Vision Pro. Pundits can't help but declare it dead at least once a month and Apple's internal shifts don't help matters.

Regardless of what conjecture can be made or small details leak out, Apple has a near-infinite cash runway for toying around with projects regardless of how successful they might be. Apple Vision Pro could truly be a money sink for Apple, but their priorities for the future mean that it doesn't matter.

I'm confident that spatial computing is what's next in computing, at least as an alternative platform. The iPad previously represented a future of computing that's still taking shape, but visionOS looks out even further than that.

See, at one point we believed that computing would be terminal-based where your account existed no matter which device you sat down at. That ultimately came to pass thanks to the internet and cloud-based accounts.

Apple Vision Pro review: hardware that's ahead of its time

The iPad took that idea and flipped it. Instead of many access terminals with multiple powerful computers, you have one computer, a naked robotic core, and transport it between terminals that have no computer present.

Whatever accessory you attach to the iPad transformed it into the computer you needed, be it a gaming console, writing terminal, laptop, sketchpad, or reading tablet — it did it all.

Apple Vision Pro removes the terminal altogether, though there will be times you'll want a classic keyboard and trackpad setup. Spatial computing means that the computer appears wherever you might be looking whenever you need it, which means the compute unit is worn on the person instead of being carried.

It takes the naked robotic core concept and kind of turns it inside out. It no longer involves attaching accessories to create the computing environment you need, but using accessories to attach information.

Once visionOS can find its way into a routinely wearable AR display, we'll see a hybrid reality where iPhones and iPads are still used, but the AR view can extend content outside of the physical glass. Apple Vision Pro is the first step in that direction because it fakes the AR we're aiming for.

Apple Vision Pro review: glasses are Apple's goal

Apple Vision Pro needed to release and exist so Apple could develop visionOS in public. It needed an audience of users and developers at a scale wider than those found at Apple Park to push the technology forward.

In the short term, I believe Apple has accomplished what it wanted with Apple Vision Pro. The M5 model likely only exists because enough people, especially enterprise, still buy the headset and Apple didn't want to make another batch of M2 chips, given the state of the chipmaking industry right now.

It isn't as if Apple merely slapped the chipset in and called it a day. Work had to go into optimizing the hardware for the new chip beyond simple speed increases.

Apple Vision Pro review: chipset upgrades helped push the platform forward and keep it modern

Real advantages were gained because of the chip upgrade, and more benefits can be found in AI, gaming, and graphics applications as time moves forward. Even the Developer Strap saw a speed upgrade for tethered operations.

I don't think we'll see another iteration of this headset, though rumors have been wishy-washy on the topic. Apple will inevitably create the next-generation model with a thinner, lighter frame that is hopefully marginally less expensive.

Such a device is coming. Patents and rumors continue to point to such a product being in the pipeline, but component suppliers can't meet the need just yet.

Even Sony struggled to make enough displays for the initial product launch. That's just how far ahead the Apple Vision Pro was in 2024 and continues to be today.

Apple Vision Pro review: It's just the beginning of Apple's spatial computing platform

Until the technology can catch up to Apple's ambitions, I think it makes sense to redistribute engineers to more imminent products. Clearly, in its current form, software, gaming, and immersive video aren't worth the effort for the audience size, so downsizing there makes some sense too.

That doesn't mean we won't see new content for those categories, just less direct from Apple. Really, we don't even know who was laid off. It could have been product managers, engineers, or even just evangelists — it's only about 60 people in a team of hundreds.

For now, Apple is pushing for smart glasses and AirPods with cameras. Both products will benefit from more development in AI and spatial computing, even if they don't run visionOS directly.

Rumors place a next-generation Apple Vision Pro somewhere around 2028 or early 2029. I'll continue to cover visionOS releases and point out specific upgrades and apps as they come in.

The Mac is a powerhouse capable of doing most anything you throw at it. Developers, writers, movie producers, and most anyone can do their work with a Mac.

Apple Vision Pro review: for the crazy ones

Go down a rung and you're at iPad. For most it's a consumption device, but for a slice of the Apple-faithful population, it's a more whimsical production platform that's way more interesting than a Mac. Our naked robotic core.

Then there's Apple Vision Pro. It's truly the device for the crazy ones, especially if you buy one today at $3,699.

If Apple Vision Pro with M5 warrants another review check in, I'll be here, hopefully with some good news. Until then, I'll continue to put on Apple Vision Pro on a regular basis to relive memories, watch 3D movies, and play the occasional game.

Oh, and of course, get some work done. This entire review was written while wearing the Apple Vision Pro and my neck doesn't even hurt.

items.title: There are features in iPhone Duo that Apple didn't talk about
items.content_html:
Now that the iPhone Duo is at least partially out in the wild, the horde of reviewers that have used the device are finding things that were previously unannounced and undiscovered. Here are a few examples.

On September 9, Apple officially entered the folding smartphone market with its iPhone Duo. While customers won't be able to get their hands on one until October 23, select reviewers have already shared their thoughts on Apple's first foldable.

Alongside the usual opinions, many of these early reviews also detail obscure iPhone Duo features. For instance, when unfolded, the iPhone Duo supports Edge Light. In essence, the outermost area of the iPhone Duo's internal display acts as a ring light during FaceTime video calls.

This capability was previously exclusive to Macs with an Apple Silicon chip, which gained Edge Light with macOS Tahoe 26.2. This makes the iPhone Duo the first iPhone with Edge Light support. It's a nice touch for the foldable, but Edge Light is far from the only thing Apple customized for the iPhone Duo.

Because the iPhone Duo is similar in size to the iPad mini when unfolded, Apple opted to include a horizontal version of Reachability. Introduced in 2014, Reachability is an Accessibility feature that makes user interface elements near the top of an iPhone screen easier to access.

On the iPhone 6 and newer models, users can swipe down on the bottom edge of their iPhone screen to temporarily move the top of the iOS UI toward the lower half of the screen. This capability is available both on the iOS Home Screen and within applications.

With the iPhone Duo, the feature will seemingly work the same way, only with the left or right side of its displays. In essence, swiping towards the edge of the screen might move half of the on-screen UI to the left or right. Wired reports that the iPhone Duo will get reachability "later this year," per Apple.

Another capability launched with iPhone Duo is the Smart Take feature. Apple says the iPhone Duo "can detect when everyone is ready and takes the picture." This means no hassle with timers and no pushing buttons to take a picture with the iPhone Duo. It's also possible to use the outer display as a live viewfinder feed when taking photos.

Additionally, the iPhone Duo will gain Apple Pencil support with the upcoming iOS 27.2 update. The capability is already available with the release candidate build of iOS 27.2, which arrived on Monday.

However, while the iPhone Duo is undoubtedly full of useful product-specific UI enhancements, you'll only find them in Apple's apps, at least for the time being. Many third-party applications have yet to implement proper display support for the iPhone Duo's display aspect ratios.

As Engadget notes, many third-party apps viewed through the iPhone Duo's inner display only occupy the central area of the screen, leaving huge black bars on the right and left sides. Some applications, like Slack, however, have already addressed this issue.

Software-related details like these are eventually going to get fixed, but that won't be the case for the iPhone Duo's hardware. Some reviewers, like Arun Maini, have noted that desktop MagSafe chargers make the iPhone tip or rotate when the device is unfolded

Still, MagSafe is an entirely optional feature on the iPhone Duo. Apple's foldable can obviously be charged via USB-C, so the device won't tip over on its own. Overall, Apple still has a few kinks to work out with the iPhone Duo, and the product isn't for everyone, regardless of all the exclusive features it offers.
